title: SYSK Selects: Lab-grown meat: Order up!
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on lab-grown (in vitro, cultured) meat, originally aired December 2012. Josh introduces the rerun, noting progress but a long way to go. The hosts cover the 2008 PETA one-million-dollar prize for commercially viable cultured meat, Willem van Eelen-style history via Winston Churchill's 1931 prediction, Morris Benjaminson's goldfish-muscle experiment, Mark Post's Dutch team making cow stem-cell muscle strips, Gabor Forgacs of Modern Meadows and his 3D-printing approach, cost estimates versus conventional beef, environmental benefits (greenhouse gases, land, water, grain), hurdles like blood, fat and taste, and early uses such as leather. The episode closes with listener mail from Colin, a Texas high school senior, and a teaser for a future factory farming episode.

segments.title: Rerun introduction and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on lab-grown meat, noting it first aired December 2012 and that progress has been made but much remains. The hosts banter about the prior podcast and set up the topic.

segments.title: PETA prize and the first in vitro hamburger
segments.summary: PETA posted a one-million-dollar reward in 2008 for a commercially viable lab-grown meat by June 2012, which was not met. A taste test of an in vitro hamburger took place in October, led by Gabor Forgacs of the University of Missouri and his company Modern Meadows; Mark Post of Maastricht in the Netherlands is the other leading researcher. Forgacs ate a sample on stage at TED Med in 2011.

segments.title: History: Churchill's prediction and Benjaminson's goldfish meat
segments.summary: Winston Churchill predicted people would grow chicken parts separately rather than whole chickens, roughly twenty years off. Morris Benjaminson of Yeshiva-type college New York Toro College grew goldfish muscle tissue in fetal bovine serum, which gained mass, and he tried to cook it. Animal rights groups responded to the idea.

segments.title: Cost estimates and comparison to conventional beef
segments.summary: A 2008 Norway conference study estimated manufacturing at about five thousand dollars a ton. Rough calculations compared cost of raising beef in Illinois with a retail markup, arriving near eleven dollars a pound. The hosts compare this to filet and Kobe beef pricing and lobster prices.

segments.title: How the meat is made, hurdles, and early products
segments.summary: The Dutch team grows cow stem cells into small muscle strips lacking blood, fat and veins, so the taste is bland. Modern Meadows considers 3D printing layers of bio-ink. Hurdles include nutrient mixtures and cost; Post's first burger was estimated at a very high price. Forgacs sees it as a niche, with leather as a likely first product and flour-like ingredients for meatballs.

segments.title: Environmental and demand arguments
segments.summary: Lab-grown meat could cut greenhouse gases substantially, use far less land and water, and be more energy efficient than livestock, which contribute significantly to global emissions. Meat demand is projected to rise with incomes in China and India, and land for grazing is limited.

segments.title: Health benefits and consumer acceptance
segments.summary: Jason Matheny of New Harvest said lab-grown meat could be healthier because pathogens are easier to control and fat content could be controlled. The hosts discuss whether people will accept fake meat and whether they would try it.

segments.title: Listener mail from Colin and upcoming factory farming episode
segments.summary: Colin, a Texas high school senior in an independent study mentorship program, thanks the show for helping with school research. The hosts mention a future factory farming episode and share social media and email contact info, then point listeners to HowStuffWorks for more.
